text:
A federal judge in the Washington D.C. District Court issued a court order on May 13, 2026, temporarily blocking the Trump Administration’s sanctions on Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories. But the Trump Administration was able to reimpose these measures just one week later after the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals issued an order staying the lower court’s ruling. The Trump Administration has also appealed the DC District Court judge’s order.

Albanese was sanctioned by the Trump Administration nearly a year ago for communicating with the International Criminal Court (ICC) on promoting international rule of law and calling for accountability for war crimes potentially committed by U.S. and Israeli individuals in Gaza.

C&SN is currently writing a detailed legal analysis on this court battle, which could prove to be pivotal in curtailing or empowering the Trump Administration’s strategy of using sanctions to attack its political opponents.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued sanctions on Albanese in July 2025 in retaliation for her rhetoric condemning U.S. and Israel’s conduct in Gaza and recommending that the ICC investigate war crimes against several Israeli and U.S. nationals—including executives of major Department of Defense contractors.

The sanctions on Albanese followed directives in Executive Order 14203, signed by Trump in February 2025, instructing federal agencies to impose sanctions on four key ICC judges as well as individuals who “directly engage” or provide “material support” to the ICC’s efforts to investigate or prosecute individuals without the consent of their country.

Executive Order 14203 significantly escalates the weaponization of sanctions against political opponents and creates a chilling effect on civil society engaging with the ICC.

“Fear of these hefty penalties can deter U.S.-based NGOs from assisting or even communicating with sanctioned ICC staff, effectively stifling documentation of human rights abuses, fact-finding missions, or legal collaboration,” C&SN warned.

Three prominent human rights organizations working in Palestine have already been sanctioned for collaborating with the ICC on investigations.

Secretary Rubio claimed that Albanese had directly engaged with the ICC to “investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute nationals of the United States or Israel, without the consent of those two countries.” Neither the U.S. nor Israel is party to the Rome Statute, which establishes the ICC’s jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

The Trump Administration has construed the ICC’s investigation of war crimes in Gaza as “lawfare” threatening U.S. national interest and sovereignty, and accused Albanese of antisemitism and conspiring against the U.S. and Israel.

To punish the ICC and discourage collaboration with the institution, President Trump has leveraged the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to impose sanctions on persons or entities deemed a “threat to national security”—which they have stretched to include the ICC investigating U.S. and Israeli officials.

Sanctions are designed to economically isolate their targets, with strict penalties—including potential criminal liability and hefty fines—for those found to have provided “material support” to designated individuals and entities.

Albanese has described how the sanctions have locked her family out of international banking systems, prevented them from visiting the U.S. where they continue to hold property (their daughter is also a U.S. citizen), caused health insurance providers to deny payments, and led hotels and venues where she was set to speak to cancel without explanation.

But in February of 2026, Albanese’s husband and daughter sued the Trump Administration, claiming the sanctions had violated their constitutional rights (Albanese was unable to bring the suit herself due to her official diplomatic role at the UN.)

Then on May 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, who is overseeing the case, ordered a temporary block on the sanctions and wrote in the court’s opinion that the sanctions impeded Albanese’s First Amendment rights.

Leon explained that Albanese’s recommendations to the ICC were “nothing more than her opinion” rather than having a binding effect on the court’s actions to prosecute or investigate U.S. or Israeli nationals.

“Not only do defendants seek to regulate Albanese’s speech, but they want to regulate her speech because of the ‘idea or message expressed,’” wrote Leon in a 26-page decision.

“Protecting the freedom of speech is ‘always’ in the public interest,” he continued, “That is so even when an individual’s views are ‘hurtful,’ ‘caustic,’ or ‘even outrageous.’”

The Trump Administration argued that Albanese should not be afforded First Amendment protections because she is not a U.S. citizen and currently resides in Tunisia—and issued her statements leading to her sanctions from abroad.

However, Leon found that her “extensive connections” to the U.S., including owning property in Washington D.C. and her daughter holding U.S. citizenship, were enough to give her claims to free speech protections.

The Trump Administration also argued that General Licenses issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which permit certain activities with sanctioned individuals, as well as a special “Parental License” specific to permitting Albanese’s interactions with her daughter, ensured the sanctions did not infringe on constitutional rights.

Leon was unconvinced by this argument, and contended that the vague permissions in the licenses failed to address the larger chilling effects caused by the sanctions which impede on the constitutional rights of Albanese and her family—such as effectively barring their daughter from entering the U.S. where she is a citizen.

The Trump Administration appealed the order from Leon. Then, the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit issued an administrative stay of Leon’s ruling pending appeal, allowing the Trump Administration to redesignate Albanese. The administrative stay does not indicate how the appeals court will judge the Trump Administration’s broader appeal to halt Leon’s court order on the sanctions.

C&SN continues to monitor this case and will write a detailed legal analysis in the future.

The Trump Administration’s sanctions targeting the ICC and those collaborating with the institution is a clear example of weaponizing national security measures against political opponents.

In 2025, C&SN launched the Civil Society Rights and Resiliency Project designed to equip nonprofits with legal tools, rapid response resources, and community wisdom to build their capacity and help them respond to this unprecedented crackdown on civil society, including through sanctions
